# Async and concurrency

<!-- Generated by `npm run train` from the sources each rule cites. To change a rule for good, change its source or say so in training/feedback.md; the next training run regenerates this file. -->

- **Build every check-then-act on shared state as one atomic operation in the shared store. Replay, nonce and idempotency guards use an atomic add-if-absent. A single-use record (state, one-time code, login transaction, invitation) is consumed with an atomic take (read-and-delete) after every check passes and before its effect runs. Shared counters and quotas use an atomic increment-and-compare made before the work starts, and they count what was requested, not what later succeeded. Never write any of these as a read followed by a separate write or remove.** With get-then-set or get-then-remove, two concurrent requests on one replica, or on two replicas that share a store, can both pass, so a proof is accepted twice or a quota is overshot. Taking the record before validation would also burn the record of a request that is then refused. *Check:* Look for a get or contains followed by a set, add or remove on replay, nonce, single-use or quota state, for these guards built on `IDistributedCache`, for counts incremented after the work based on its outcome, and for takes made before validation. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity ADR-1198; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Update a shared or durable record that concurrent requests may change with a versioned compare-and-replace, or with the row's optimistic concurrency token. On a conflict, reload and decide again, a bounded number of times, and let the exception propagate after the last attempt. Never overwrite it unconditionally, and don't treat a conflict as the adverse outcome (such as token reuse) without re-reading first. When a durable row already exists, make the single-use spend atomic through that row's concurrency token instead of tracking the same state in a second store.** Unconditional writes lose concurrent updates. A conflict may only mean another writer touched the row, so deciding without a re-read gets it wrong. A second store would have to stay in agreement with the row. *Check:* Look for plain sets on shared session or state records, retries on version conflicts with no limit, concurrency exceptions that go straight to a revoke or reuse branch, and single-use state for a durable row that is duplicated in a cache or expiring key set. *Note:* Also fail closed when the shared store fails, and encrypt shared values that hold secrets. <sub>Identity ADR-1164; Identity ADR-1192; Identity ADR-1217; Identity ADR-1290; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **When a request and a background pass, or two concurrent requests, can act on the same record, make the state transition an atomic claim. Check the precondition against the stored value inside the update, report whether this call made the change, and have only the call that won perform the follow-up effects (notifications, token delivery, audit, logs). Build those effects from the record as it was claimed, not from an earlier read. Put the transition in one shared helper that both paths call, and revoke dependent records in the same unit of work as the claim.** Otherwise two concurrent approvals or terminations both run their effects, so parties are notified twice. Payloads built from an earlier read also miss changes that landed in between, such as a client added to a session that gets no logout notification. *Check:* Look for transitions that check status on an earlier read, update methods that return void instead of whether they won, effects dispatched without checking the claim result (for example a revoke that returns null or false), effects built from an earlier read, and termination logic duplicated between a request path and a background job. *Note:* An approval also validates the approving subject first, and denies the request if the subject is refused. <sub>Identity ADR-1085; Identity ADR-1112; Identity ADR-1222; Identity ADR-1223; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make the update function passed to a read-modify-write operation decide only from its argument, the value as stored, and give it no side effects.** The operation calls the function again whenever a save loses a race. A function that uses state captured from an earlier read, or that has side effects, acts on stale data or acts more than once. *Check:* In update lambdas, look for values captured from a read made before the call, and for I/O, notifications, deliveries, outcome logging or changes to outer state. <sub>Identity ADR-1222</sub>
- **In production code, don't let correctness depend on process-local state. Put durable state in the database and shared short-lived state in a distributed shared-state store, so any replica can serve any request without session affinity. Endpoints that cooperate across requests, such as a verification endpoint and a polling endpoint, share state only through the persisted record. Don't compare against an in-memory copy of a previous configuration, and don't run work inside a request that grows with the number of stored records.** Services run as interchangeable, disposable replicas. State in one process is invisible to the other replicas and is lost when the replica is replaced, and replicas apply changes at different moments. *Check:* Look for static or singleton dictionaries, caches, queues or job stores that hold state other requests or replicas depend on, for designs that need sticky sessions, for cleanup that compares against a remembered in-memory set, and for request handlers that scan all stored records. <sub>Identity ADR-1059; Identity ADR-1134; Identity ADR-1443; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Enforce a rate limit or quota that is meant to hold across the deployment through a store shared by all replicas, not through per-process limiters such as `System.Threading.RateLimiting` partitions registered with `AddRateLimiter`. Where the repository has a shared limiter, declare the limit for it to judge instead of calling counter operations from an endpoint.** A limiter whose state lives in one process admits N times its limit on N replicas. *Check:* Look for deployment-wide limits or quotas built on in-process counters or `AddRateLimiter` partitions, and for endpoints that drive counters directly to enforce a limit. <sub>Identity ADR-1246; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, run work that follows a committed change, or that must not be left half-done, on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by its own timeout through the injected `TimeProvider`, not on the request's or host's token. This covers cache eviction, change announcements, ending sessions, clearing counters, observer notifications, audit records and their lookups, and the write-back after a state-changing remote call such as a refresh-token rotation. Start this work only after the commit, log its failures instead of throwing them, and put a required announcement in a `finally` so a failed publish doesn't skip it.** A client that disconnects or a host that stops after the commit would otherwise cancel the follow-up, leaving stale caches, live sessions, missing audit records or a lost rotated token. An exception would turn a successful write into an error, and unbounded `None` would let a hung store hold the request open. *Check:* After `SaveChangesAsync`, a commit or a state-changing remote call, look for follow-up calls passed `HttpContext.RequestAborted`, the request token or `stoppingToken`, for `CancellationToken.None` with no timeout, for observer or audit calls made before the commit, and for follow-up exceptions that reach the caller. *Note:* Put the bounded token inside the shared recorder or helper, so no call site can drop the record. <sub>Identity ADR-1229; Identity ADR-1230; Identity ADR-1351; Identity ADR-1407; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity review of #420; Identity outcomes of #551; Identity outcomes of #620</sub>
- **Keep the request's cancellation token on work that runs before the commit, or that is itself the requested operation, such as an idempotent revoke endpoint. Don't report these steps for using the request token.** That work is not post-commit. If it fails, the caller can repeat the request. *Check:* Report pre-commit steps only if they wrongly use the post-commit bounded helper, not for using the request's token. <sub>Identity ADR-1351; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Run a repair or compensating action that follows a failed operation on a fresh bounded `CancellationToken`, not on the token of the operation that may have timed out.** If the failure came from that token's timeout, the repair throws `OperationCanceledException` at once, never runs, and leaves the state broken. *Check:* In catch blocks that revert or repair state, look for repair calls that reuse the caller's or the timed-out token instead of a new `CancellationTokenSource` with a timeout. <sub>Identity outcomes of #553</sub>
- **Record a refused credential's failure count on `CancellationToken.None`, before auditing the refusal.** A client that disconnects right after submitting a guess must not avoid the count, even when the audit recorder honours the request's cancellation. *Check:* Look for failure-recording calls that pass the request or `HttpContext` token, or that run after the audit call. <sub>Identity ADR-1237; Identity ADR-1399</sub>
- **Write every catch filter so that only a cancellation the relevant token requested is treated as cancellation: `catch (Exception e) when (e is not OperationCanceledException || !token.IsCancellationRequested)`. The relevant token is the stopping token in a background loop and the caller's token in a fallback or fan-out catch. Treat any other `OperationCanceledException` or `TaskCanceledException`, such as an `HttpClient` or store timeout, as an ordinary failure: log it, then fall back, retry, or run the remaining handlers.** A filter on the exception type alone lets a timeout escape. That skips the fallback and ends a `BackgroundService`, which stops the host under the default `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior.StopHost`. A filter on the token alone lets any ordinary handler failure escape once the token is cancelled, so the remaining handlers never run. *Check:* Look for `catch (OperationCanceledException)` that rethrows or breaks unconditionally, filters such as `when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)` with no token check, and filters in fan-out loops that test the token but not the exception type. <sub>Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1242; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #465; Identity outcomes of #491; Identity outcomes of #617</sub>
- **When a catch block handles failures during an operation, such as start-up loading, dispose what the operation acquired, and rethrow a requested cancellation as the original `OperationCanceledException` without wrapping it in a domain exception.** Wrapping the cancellation turns a shutdown during start-up into a reported load failure. *Check:* Look for catch blocks that wrap every exception in a domain exception without excluding `OperationCanceledException`, or that skip cleanup on cancellation. <sub>Identity outcomes of #709</sub>
- **When concurrent callers share one in-flight retrieval (single-flight), run the shared work once, without any caller's `CancellationToken`, bounded by its own configured timeout, and on its own copy of any disposable input a caller owns (such as an `X509Certificate2` chain). Have each caller stop waiting with `.WaitAsync(cancellationToken)`. Record the result or failure in the caches before removing the in-flight entry, and key the entry and any remembered failure by the input plus the limits applied to it (timeout, size cap), not by the URL alone.** A caller that cancels or disposes its input must not break the work for the other callers. Removing the entry early lets a duplicate fetch start. A key without the limits lets a caller with a short timeout fail another caller's fetch and block it with the remembered failure. *Check:* In single-flight code, look for a caller's token captured in the shared delegate, a missing timeout, references to caller-owned disposables, removal of the entry before the cache write, and keys that hold only the URI when limits vary per caller. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1315; Identity ADR-1400; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity outcomes of #484</sub>
- **When a cache wraps a single-flight retrieval, check the value cache and the remembered-failure cache before joining the single-flight, and again inside the shared delegate, returning what they hold without fetching.** A caller delayed between the outer check and `GetOrAdd` can otherwise start a new fetch just after another fetch recorded its result, and immediately fetch again from a source that just failed. The outer check still lets a cached answer skip the single-flight. *Check:* Look for `GetOrAdd` with a `Lazy`/`Task` factory, or a shared-fetch delegate, that downloads unconditionally, and for an outer check removed in favour of only the inner one. <sub>Identity ADR-1106; Identity ADR-1315; Identity ADR-1400; Identity outcomes of #480</sub>
- **Share remote fetches through the repository's shared single-flight helper instead of new hand-written `ConcurrentDictionary` and `Lazy<Task>` bookkeeping, and have each owner create its own instance rather than resolving the helper as a DI singleton.** A copy of the bookkeeping misses fixes made to the shared helper, and a singleton mixes the keys of unrelated features in one dictionary. *Check:* Look for new in-flight task dictionaries for remote fetches, and for DI registrations of the single-flight helper. <sub>Identity ADR-1315</sub>
- **Refresh a rotating refresh token single-flight across the whole cluster: take a per-session lock and a cluster-wide lease. Once the lease is won, run the token request and the write-back of the rotated token on `CancellationToken.None`, bounded by the client's timeout. If the lease can't be taken in time, fail with 503. Never send the same refresh token in a second refresh, and don't turn off rotation or rely on a reuse grace window at the provider instead.** Presenting a rotated refresh token twice trips reuse detection, and the provider revokes the whole token family. Rotation is a defence RFC 9700 §4.14.2 recommends. *Check:* Look for refresh code that uses only an in-process lock or no lock, for retry or fallback branches that resend the old token, for the request token passed to the refresh call or its persistence, and for configuration that turns off rotation or adds a grace window. <sub>Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Release a distributed lease with an atomic compare-and-remove against a random owner token that the acquirer stored as the lease value. Never release with an unconditional delete, a version match, or a read followed by a separate delete. Release as soon as the work ends, in a `finally` block on `CancellationToken.None`, and log a failed release as a warning without replacing the work's own result or exception.** A delete can remove a lease another replica took after yours expired. An expiring store restarts a re-added key at version one, so versions can't tell the two apart. A lease left until expiry makes the other replicas wait, and a failed release must not hide the real outcome, since the lease expires anyway. *Check:* Look for lease release by key alone, by version, or with GET then DEL, for acquisitions without a release in `finally`, for releases that pass the caller's token, and for release exceptions that propagate. <sub>Identity ADR-1291; Identity docs/backend-for-frontend.md</sub>
- **When a periodic pass must run on only one replica per interval, take an expiring lease keyed by the interval window (UTC ticks divided by interval ticks) that lasts less than the timer period, and skip the pass if the lease is lost. Still keep the per-item work idempotent, with each entity changed in its own unit of work under its concurrency token.** Without a lease, every replica claims the same items. A lease as long as the interval is still held at the next tick, so every other pass is skipped. The lease is an optimisation, and per-entity concurrency is what keeps overlapping writers correct. *Check:* In background services on multi-replica hosts, look for passes with no lease, a lease that never expires or lasts at least the timer period, or per-item work that assumes it is the only runner. <sub>Identity ADR-1223; Identity ADR-1404</sub>
- **Converge derived state through an idempotent reconciliation pass. The pass reads the persisted store, compares it with a durably recorded last-reconciled input, and repairs what differs. It runs at host start and after every change, and the unit of work that changes the input marks the record stale. Run the pass under a lease keyed by the input's content fingerprint and its row concurrency token. A replica that can't take the lease leaves the work to the holder and retries after a configurable delay. Don't maintain the state by replaying events or draining an in-memory queue.** Queued jobs and in-memory events are lost on restart, while reconciliation can be rerun safely. A key without the concurrency token would skip a change back to an earlier state. *Check:* Look for derived state updated only by queued jobs or events, passes that read in-process state, passes that don't run at start-up, passes without a durable record or lease, and lease keys that hash only the content. <sub>Identity ADR-1412; Identity ADR-1443; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't rely on a non-durable dispatcher, job queue or broadcast alone for work that must eventually happen, such as rotation, rewrapping or cleanup. Back it with a periodic pass under a distributed lease, and use the dispatched job only to make the work happen sooner.** The dispatcher isn't durable, so the leased pass is the path that guarantees the work. *Check:* Look for required maintenance that is triggered only by a dispatched job or a broadcast. <sub>Identity ADR-1407</sub>
- **Hand work to the background as a snapshot of what it needs (ids, actor, request and trace context) captured when the event is published. Never pass `HttpContext`, `IHttpContextAccessor` or request-scoped services to a handler, sink or background job.** Handlers and sinks may run after the request has ended, when the `HttpContext` and the request scope are no longer valid. *Check:* Look for event handlers, audit sinks or background jobs that read `IHttpContextAccessor`, `HttpContext` or request-scoped state, and for event envelopes filled in after publishing. <sub>Identity ADR-1047; Identity ADR-1283; Identity docs/audit-records.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Run deferred jobs from a bounded `Channel<T>` with a fixed number of consumer loops, each item in its own `CreateAsyncScope()` under the app's stopping token, logging a failed item and moving on. Enqueue without blocking the producing request (for example `ChannelWriter.TryWrite`), and log a job that is dropped because the queue is full. Don't consume the queue with `Parallel.ForEachAsync` or with a single sequential consumer.** An exception in one `Parallel.ForEachAsync` body cancels every running job, and a single consumer lets one slow job delay the rest. Unbounded queues exhaust memory, and out-of-band work must not stall or fail the request that triggered it. *Check:* Look for `Parallel.ForEachAsync` over `ReadAllAsync`, unbounded channels, `await writer.WriteAsync` on a request path, enqueue failures that reach the caller, drops that aren't logged, and one failure that stops a batch. <sub>Identity ADR-1242; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **Make every deferred-job handler idempotent on the dispatch identifier and thread-safe when it is registered as a singleton. Throw when a step it depends on fails, so the dispatcher retries the job.** Dispatch is at least once: a retry runs every handler of the job again, and several consumers can run the same singleton at once. A swallowed failure loses the retry. *Check:* Look for sends or writes in job handlers that aren't safe to repeat for the same dispatch id, mutable instance state in singleton handlers without synchronisation, and caught-and-ignored failures of required reads. <sub>Identity ADR-1242; Identity ADR-1478</sub>
- **Deliver notifications to third parties, such as back-channel logout to relying parties, out of band through the deferred job dispatcher, not inline in the request.** A failed delivery can then be retried, and delivery doesn't depend on the request or the browser. *Check:* Look for request-pipeline code that calls a relying party's `backchannel_logout_uri` or another third-party endpoint directly. <sub>Identity ADR-1380</sub>
- **A hosted service whose `StopAsync` does work, such as a final flush of buffered data, does it exactly once and never throws. Memoize the stop task under a `Lock` so repeated or concurrent stops await the same task, serialize it with the periodic work, track shared counts with `Interlocked`, and log as a warning, with a defined event id, any data it couldn't save or still held when the stop token expired.** The host may stop a service twice at once and dispose services while the other stop is still writing. A second flush would race the batch, and an exception disrupts the shutdown of other services. *Check:* Look for `StopAsync` overrides without a run-once guard, without serialization against the timer loop, that can throw, or that drop data silently when the stop times out. <sub>Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1303; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Run periodic background work on a `PeriodicTimer` created with the injected `TimeProvider`, with its period bound from validated options. Catch and log a failed pass and continue at the next tick, honour the host's stopping token, and don't throw from `ExecuteAsync` when the host stops.** One failed pass must not end the loop. Shutdown must be clean so rollouts lose no work, and timing must stay testable. *Check:* Look for `Task.Delay` loops, `System.Threading.Timer`, `new PeriodicTimer(interval)` without the `TimeProvider`, `TimeProvider.System` used directly, hard-coded periods, loop bodies without a catch-and-log, and an `OperationCanceledException` that escapes on stop. <sub>Identity ADR-1134; Identity ADR-1199; Identity ADR-1223</sub>
- **When a periodic flush fails, keep the failed batch at the head of the queue and retry it first, holding new data in the accumulator until the queue is empty.** Memory stays bounded, and a later batch never commits before an earlier one. *Check:* Look for failed batches that are dropped, re-queued at the tail, or that let the queue grow without bound. <sub>Identity ADR-1199</sub>
- **Make a cross-replica change announcement carry only a hint that identifies what changed, and have the receiver re-read the committed state. Apply a change locally first and publish only after the write commits, logging a failed publish instead of throwing. Handlers must be idempotent and correct when a message is lost, repeated, late, out of order, or is the replica's own message.** Delivery is best effort, at most once and unordered, so a payload can be stale and convergence can't depend on delivery. *Check:* Look for broadcast messages that carry settings or entity payloads, receivers that apply message contents, publishes made before the commit, publish exceptions that reach the caller, and handlers with counters, toggles or work that breaks on a second call. Evictions and re-reads are fine. <sub>Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **A replica cache kept fresh by broadcasts must also re-read on missed-message notifications, by dropping or revalidating everything a lost message could have made stale, and must refresh entries older than a configured interval. Its subscriber hands messages to handlers off the connection's receive loop, reconciles once the subscription takes effect and again after every reconnect, and retries subscribing while the server is unreachable.** Lost broadcasts would otherwise leave a replica stale forever. A slow handler must not block the receive loop, and messages published before the subscription or during a disconnect never arrive. *Check:* Look for broadcast-only caches with no load timestamp or refresh interval, handlers that ignore reconnects or missed messages, handlers awaited inline in the message callback, and subscribe calls with no retry. <sub>Identity ADR-1205; Identity ADR-1407; Identity ADR-1412; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Keep cache loads and evictions consistent under concurrency. Don't store a load that an eviction overtook, and apply the same eviction guard before recording a failure. Clear a source cache, and await it, before clearing a cache derived from it. Publish related data, such as a certificate and its issuer chain, as one entry or only once every part is complete.** A stale load or failure written after an eviction brings back an old key or refuses requests for a whole retry interval. A derived entry built between two clears is rebuilt from stale data, and a reader that sees partial data builds something broken. *Check:* Look for cache writes that don't check an eviction counter or version on both the success and failure paths, clears in reverse dependency order or fired without awaiting, and two cache writes where the first is visible before the second. <sub>Identity ADR-1235; Identity review of #420; Identity outcomes of #555; Identity outcomes of #572</sub>
- **Don't zero cached key material when it is evicted. Zero it only when the owning cache is disposed.** An earlier consumer may still be using the key, and zeroing it would corrupt operations in flight. *Check:* Look for key caches that clear or zero buffers in their eviction path. <sub>Identity ADR-1235</sub>
- **Create a lazily initialised shared client so that a failed creation is not cached and the next call tries again.** A transient failure during creation must not break every later call for the life of the process. *Check:* Look for `Lazy<T>` with exception caching, or a cached `Task`, that keeps a faulted result. <sub>Identity ADR-1260</sub>
- **Serialise per-resource work inside a process with per-key locks that are reference-counted and removed when the last waiter leaves, not with striped locks, whenever the lock may be held across a long wait. Key the locks by purpose as well as entity when a holder can call another service that locks the same entity. Bound every wait with a configured timeout that ends in a defined error, and release the lock in `finally` or `Dispose` when the holder is cancelled.** A stripe held while waiting on a remote lease blocks unrelated keys. A shared key makes nested operations wait on themselves, and unbounded waits or locks never released block every later caller. *Check:* Look for `SemaphoreSlim` stripes or lock arrays held across remote calls or polling, per-key lock dictionaries that never remove entries, locks keyed only by entity id across nested services, waits with no timeout, and cancellation paths that don't release. <sub>Identity ADR-1291; Identity ADR-1381; Identity review of #420</sub>
- **Protect shared mutable state against concurrent access, and release subscriptions and disposables so they don't leak. A hosted service stores its `ChangeToken.OnChange` or `RegisterChangeCallback` registrations and disposes them on stop and on dispose.** Unsynchronised shared state races, and undisposed registrations keep firing callbacks and keep the service alive after the host stops. *Check:* Look for non-thread-safe collections or fields changed from several threads, event handlers that are never unsubscribed, disposables never disposed, and change-token registrations that aren't stored and disposed. <sub>NCodeGroup maintainer: principal-engineer-review; Identity ADR-1433</sub>
- **In production code, link the cancellation source of any background loop or watch started for a SignalR or other long-lived connection to the connection's `ConnectionAborted` token.** A watch registered as the connection drops would otherwise never be cancelled, and would keep polling the store for a dead connection. *Check:* Look for per-connection `CancellationTokenSource`s or tasks created in hub filters or `OnConnectedAsync` that are cancelled only from `OnDisconnectedAsync`. <sub>Identity outcomes of #607</sub>
- **Don't read `HttpContext` or `IHttpContextAccessor` in code that runs in an interactive Blazor Server component or circuit. Take the user from the circuit's authentication state or a connection-scoped session instead.** Microsoft documents `IHttpContextAccessor` as unavailable in interactive components, and the hub's response has already started by the time a component runs. *Check:* Look for `IHttpContextAccessor` injected into, or `HttpContext` used by, Razor components, circuit handlers or per-circuit services. <sub>Identity ADR-1435</sub>
- **When a shared `CancellationTokenSource` signals an event that other components watch, such as a session ending, latch it once so every watcher learns of it together, and signal it without running the callbacks inside the caller (for example `CancelAsync` rather than `Cancel`), while making sure `IsCancellationRequested` is set before the call returns. Don't add a separate detection loop for each watcher.** Watchers must not run inside the caller that detected the event, a later check must see it at once, and separate loops each notice it up to one interval late. *Check:* Look for `Cancel()` on shared signals called from request or invocation paths, code that detects the event without signalling the latch, and new per-caller revalidation loops. <sub>Identity ADR-1441</sub>
- **Hold an ambient scope that DbContext query filters read, such as the current tenant, in an `AsyncLocal<T>`-backed accessor, not in DI-scoped state or `HttpContext`.** Contexts that `IDbContextFactory` creates from the root provider live outside the current DI scope, so their queries would run without the scope. *Check:* Look for query-filter scope stored in a scoped service or in `HttpContext` where contexts may come from `IDbContextFactory`. <sub>Identity ADR-1018</sub>
- **At logout, first remove the server-side session and delete the cookie on `CancellationToken.None`. Then revoke the refresh token (RFC 7009) on `CancellationToken.None` bounded by a timeout, and log any failure, a cancellation included, without failing the logout.** A client that disconnects must not leave the session behind, and the user asked to leave, so the local session ends whatever happens at the provider. *Check:* Look for session removal or revocation that passes the request's token, revocation before local removal, and revocation failures that fail the logout. <sub>Identity ADR-1293</sub>
- **Sign and unwrap content keys only through asynchronous members that take a `CancellationToken` and return `ValueTask`, up through every caller, with no synchronous twin, and never block on a key management service call. Load and prove remote keys during host start-up (for example in `IHostedLifecycleService.StartingAsync`), not lazily in a synchronous provider or DI factory. Compute every signature before writing serialized output.** A remote key signs over a network call that can wait, fail or be cancelled, and a synchronous twin would work only for local keys. A broken key or missing permission should stop the host, not fail the first login. Writing output between awaits interleaves serialization with async work. *Check:* Look for synchronous sign, encode, issue or decode members, sync overloads next to async ones, `.Result` or `GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on key calls, key reads in keyed-service factories or on first use, and signing awaited inside a block of `Utf8JsonWriter` calls. <sub>Identity ADR-1471; Identity ADR-1472; Identity ADR-1479</sub>
- **In production code, give every async method you own a `ValueTask`/`ValueTask<T>` return, an `Async` suffix and a required trailing `CancellationToken`, private helpers included, and flow the caller's token into it. Return `Task` only where a framework contract fixes the shape, such as middleware `InvokeAsync`, an interface you don't own, or a method group handed directly to a framework API. Write minimal-API endpoint handlers as `ValueTask` methods with a trailing token, and have the mapping pass `httpContext.RequestAborted`.** This is NCodeGroup's async convention. A required token means a call added inside a cancellable flow can't silently drop cancellation. *Check:* Look for new async methods that return `Task` outside a framework contract, lack the `Async` suffix, or lack a trailing token. Also look for helpers that read `HttpContext.RequestAborted` or `ConnectionAborted` instead of taking a token, and methods that create their own `new CancellationTokenSource(timeout)` instead of having the caller or a shared helper pass the bounded token in. *Note:* Older guidance named minimal-API handlers as a `Task` boundary. The more recent decision converts them to the convention. Test projects are exempt: don't ask test methods, test helpers or framework overrides (xUnit tests, `WebApplicationFactory`, `HttpMessageHandler`/`AuthenticationHandler` overrides, `DisposeAsync`, `IHost` members, async lambdas passed to framework APIs) to return `ValueTask` or take a token (Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md, Identity outcomes of #590). <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity ADR-1496; Identity outcomes of #491; Identity outcomes of #580; Identity outcomes of #600</sub>
- **Don't report a required trailing `CancellationToken` on one of our own async methods as unused or misleading because none of its callees accepts a token, and don't suggest removing it, making it optional (`= default`), suppressing the analyzer, or adding `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` just to use it. Explicit `CancellationToken.None` at root call sites that have no token, such as test methods and entry points, is intended.** The token is part of the method's contract, so a call added later honours it. Adding a throw would turn work that takes no token into a cancellation point and change its behaviour. *Check:* Before reporting an unused token or repeated `CancellationToken.None`, check whether the method is ours and async and whether the caller is a root call site. If so, don't report it. Do report a caller that passes `None` while a request token is available. *Note:* Supersedes the earlier finding (Identity outcomes of #625) that asked for unused token parameters to be removed. This applies to production code and test helpers alike. <sub>Identity outcomes of #580; Identity outcomes of #732; Identity outcomes of #753</sub>
- **In production code, a method that a decision record makes uncancellable, or that runs post-commit work on its own bounded token, takes no `CancellationToken` parameter and carries a `[SuppressMessage]` whose `Justification` cites that decision record. Don't report such a method for lacking a token. Exempt methods from the async-shape analyzer only this way, never with a marker attribute, `#pragma` or an `.editorconfig` severity change.** A token parameter the method ignores would misstate its cancellation, and a token passed by the caller could drop the effect. A justified `[SuppressMessage]` records the reason next to the method instead of weakening the rule everywhere. *Check:* For an async method without a trailing token, check for a justified suppression that cites a decision record. Report suppressions with no or an empty justification, `#pragma` or `.editorconfig` changes to the async-shape diagnostics, and uncancellable methods that accept a token and ignore it. <sub>Identity ADR-1496; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Await a `ValueTask` exactly once. When a result is stored or awaited by several callers, keep it as a private field or a property holding a `Task<T>` created with `.AsTask()`, and call `.AsTask()` when passing a `ValueTask` to a `Task`-based API such as `Task.WhenAll`, rather than changing the method to return `Task`.** A `ValueTask` may be backed by a pooled source that is invalid after its first await. Converting the result keeps the method's shape while satisfying the `Task` API. *Check:* Look for a `ValueTask` awaited twice, stored and awaited by several consumers, or methods changed to return `Task` only to fit a `Task` combinator or to share a cached result. <sub>Identity ADR-1496; Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, never block on async work with `.Result`, `.Wait()` or `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`, and never write `async void` methods.** Blocking on async work and `async void` break cancellation and error propagation. *Check:* Search the diff for `.Result`, `.Wait()`, `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` and `async void`. <sub>Identity convention-audit.instructions.md</sub>
- **Offload work to another thread only when it must leave the calling thread, and then use `Task.Run`, never `Task.Factory.StartNew` with an async delegate.** `StartNew` with an async delegate returns a `Task<Task>` that doesn't represent the work, so its exceptions are lost. *Check:* Look for `Task.Factory.StartNew` given an async lambda, and for needless `Task.Run` wrapping. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp.instructions.md; Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Don't use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in code that runs only under ASP.NET Core or the generic host. In a library that UI or other context-bound apps may consume, use it on every `await`.** ASP.NET Core and the generic host install no `SynchronizationContext`, so it does nothing there, while context-bound consumers need it. *Check:* Check whether the project is host-only or a general-purpose library, then look for superfluous or missing `ConfigureAwait(false)`. <sub>Identity ADR-1285; Identity csharp.instructions.md</sub>
- **In production code, when an async method needs span or ref-struct work, do that work in a synchronous helper instead of converting to arrays or strings.** Spans and ref structs can't live across awaits. *Check:* Look for async methods that allocate arrays or strings only to avoid span restrictions. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-production.instructions.md</sub>
- **Order an outbound call's resilience strategies with the total timeout outermost, then retry, then a per-attempt timeout, and give every outbound call at least the total timeout. Time a circuit breaker on the monotonic clock (`TimeProvider.GetTimestamp`), and close it only on a success from a call made after it opened.** The total timeout bounds the whole call, and the per-attempt timeout stops a provider that never answers from using up the budget. A wall-clock step could hold a breaker open, and a slow earlier call must not undo a newer failure. *Check:* Look for a different strategy order, retried calls without a per-attempt timeout, paths with no total timeout, breakers based on `DateTimeOffset`/`UtcNow`, and close logic that doesn't compare the call's start time with the time the breaker opened. <sub>Identity ADR-1336; Identity ADR-1246</sub>
- **Run an external CLI or child process with a configurable timeout, kill its process tree when the timeout passes, report the failure, and read its output asynchronously. In a script's cleanup path, stop and dispose concurrent calls that were never received, rather than waiting for them without a timeout.** A process that hangs on a prompt or the network would block the run forever, synchronous reads of large output can deadlock, and waiting in cleanup delays reporting an earlier failure. *Check:* Look for process invocations with no time limit, no kill on timeout, or blocking reads of redirected stdout/stderr, and for `finally` blocks that receive or await runspaces, jobs or tasks with no timeout. <sub>project-template outcomes of #272; project-template outcomes of #183</sub>
- **In a GitHub Actions workflow, don't put a job that must finish in the same concurrency group as a job that sets `cancel-in-progress: true`. Give the job that must finish its own group, or make sure the cancelling trigger can't fire while it is queued or running (for example, run a comment-triggered job only when `github.event.issue.state == 'open'`).** GitHub applies the setting of the most recently queued run, and a newer run can take the group's single pending slot, so the job's work is lost and nothing retries it. `cancel-in-progress: false` doesn't protect a job from other runs. *Check:* Look for the same `concurrency.group` across jobs or workflows with different `cancel-in-progress` settings, and for triggers that can start the cancelling job while the other one runs. <sub>Identity outcomes of #436; identity-platform outcomes of #28</sub>
- **In a Helm chart, give a Deployment whose replicas keep single-use state in process the `Recreate` strategy. Use a rolling update with `maxSurge: 1` and `maxUnavailable: 0` only when that state is in a shared store.** Two replicas with in-process single-use state must never run at once, and even `maxSurge: 0` starts the new pod while the old one still serves. *Check:* Check that the strategy depends on whether a shared state store is configured, and look for rolling updates, including `maxSurge: 0`, used without one. <sub>Identity ADR-1458</sub>
- **Cap any computed `setTimeout` delay well below 2^31-1 ms, for example at the regular poll interval.** Browsers treat a larger delay as 0, so a timer that re-arms itself runs in a tight loop. *Check:* Look for `setTimeout` delays computed from a remote timestamp or lifetime with no upper bound. <sub>Identity outcomes of #606</sub>
- **In a test project, test concurrency with gates instead of timing. A stub awaits a `TaskCompletionSource`, the test asserts state while the calls wait, then releases the gate. To prove sharing, start two calls and assert a single request, then cancel the first caller and dispose its input to prove the shared work uses its own token and its own copy. To prove a limit, set it to one and assert that a second call doesn't complete while the first waits.** Without a gate the calls may not overlap, so the test proves nothing about sharing or limits. *Check:* Look for concurrency, coalescing or limit tests that rely on delays or races, and coalescing tests that don't cover cancelling the first caller. *Applies to:* `**/*.cs` <sub>Identity csharp-testing.instructions.md; Identity csharp-tests.instructions.md</sub>
- **In test scripts where concurrent processes or runspaces append to a shared log under a named mutex, catch `AbandonedMutexException` around `WaitOne` and continue, and derive the mutex name from a hash (such as SHA-256) of the log file's full path.** If a holder dies while holding the mutex, the next bare `WaitOne` throws. A name derived from the path makes every writer to the same file share one lock. *Check:* Look for `WaitOne` on a named mutex without an `AbandonedMutexException` handler, and for mutex names that are hard-coded or not derived from the full path. <sub>project-template outcomes of #258</sub>
- **Don't report an in-memory coalescing set used as a work queue as unbounded when it deduplicates by key, drops nothing, and documents that its size is bounded by the number of distinct keys.** Its memory grows with the number of distinct keys, not with the request rate. *Check:* Check whether repeated requests for the same key coalesce and whether the class summary explains the bound. <sub>Identity outcomes of #577</sub>
- **Don't report that an awaited wait in a hosted service can fault and escape `ExecuteAsync` without first checking how the awaited task completes.** A task completed only through `TrySetResult` and awaited with `WaitAsync(stoppingToken)` ends only with a result or with an already-handled cancellation, so a proposed catch would guard against nothing. *Check:* Read the awaited method's implementation (`TaskCompletionSource` use, `WaitAsync` on the stopping token) and sibling services that wait the same way before reporting. <sub>Identity outcomes of #702</sub>
- **A helper installed as an endpoint's `RequestDelegate` may return `Task` and take no `CancellationToken`, but make it private, say in its XML doc that it is the delegate's body, and test it through the method that installs it.** Matching the framework's delegate signature justifies the shape, and keeping it private and documented stops it from looking like an async helper that breaks the convention. *Check:* Look for non-private `Task`-returning methods without a token that only form a `RequestDelegate`. <sub>Identity outcomes of #710</sub>
